quiz.title: dplyr Data Manipulation Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the core dplyr verbs, the pipe and group_by. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Data manipulation with the dplyr package in R

questions.q: Which dplyr verb keeps only the rows that meet a condition?
questions.explanation: filter() subsets rows by a logical test, e.g. filter(df, age > 30). select() works on columns, not rows.

questions.q: You want to keep only the columns 'name' and 'salary'. Which verb do you use?
questions.explanation: select() chooses columns by name (or helpers like starts_with()). filter() is for rows.

questions.q: Which verb adds a new column computed from existing ones?
questions.explanation: mutate() creates or overwrites columns, e.g. mutate(df, bmi = weight / height^2), keeping all existing rows.

options: Sorts rows by score from highest to lowest
Keeps rows where score is high
questions.explanation: arrange() reorders rows; wrapping a column in desc() sorts it in descending order.

questions.q: Which verb collapses many rows into a single summary value such as a mean or count?
questions.explanation: summarise() (also spelled summarize()) reduces rows to summary statistics, e.g. summarise(df, avg = mean(score)).

questions.q: What does the pipe operator %>% do?
options: Comments out a line of code
Passes the result on its left into the first argument of the function on its right
questions.explanation: %>% (from magrittr, re-exported by dplyr) chains steps: df %>% filter(...) %>% select(...) reads left to right instead of nesting calls.

questions.q: To get the mean salary for each department, which verb do you pair with summarise()?
questions.explanation: group_by(department) splits the data into groups; summarise() then produces one summary row per group.

questions.q: Given df %>% group_by(city) %>% summarise(n = n()), what does n() return?
options: The number of columns in df
The number of rows in each city group
The sum of a numeric column
questions.explanation: n() counts rows within the current group, so you get the row count for each city.

faq.q: What are the five main verbs in dplyr?
faq.a: filter() for rows, select() for columns, mutate() to add or change columns, arrange() to sort rows, and summarise() to reduce rows to summary values. group_by() is often used with summarise() for grouped results.

faq.q: What is the pipe operator %>% and why use it?
faq.a: The pipe passes the object on its left into the next function as the first argument, so you can chain steps left to right: df %>% filter(x > 0) %>% summarise(mean(x)). It replaces deeply nested calls and reads like a sentence.

faq.q: What is the difference between filter() and select()?
faq.a: filter() keeps or drops rows based on a condition, while select() keeps or drops columns by name. One works on observations, the other on variables.

faq.q: How does group_by() change what summarise() returns?
faq.a: Without group_by(), summarise() returns one row for the whole data. With group_by(col), the data is split into groups and summarise() returns one summary row per group.
